status: wave-4: pieces occupy lattice elements (volume, face, edge), not cell slots

shapes.design_purpose: The starting shape. Two units per block equals one harvest swing, so a small shelter visibly eats into a resource node instead of feeling free.

A thin partition standing on a vertical face of the lattice, centred on the plane the two neighbouring cells share, so it belongs to neither cell and a cube can fill either side of it. Snaps to the nearest vertical face to the crosshair - no rotation key. Half the cost of a cube so walling a shelter is cheaper than filling it.

Stands on a vertical edge of the lattice - the line where up to four walls meet - so it always lines up with the panels around it and stacks on the post below when you aim at its top. Corners where walls meet grow a post visual on their own; the placed post is for free-standing frames and for making a corner load-bearing in the player's eye.

Runs along a horizontal edge of the lattice, the line a wall's top and a floor's rim share, so it reads as a lintel over a doorway, a wall plate along the top of a wall, or a rail along a slab's edge depending only on what it is next to.

A slab lying on a horizontal face of the lattice - the plane between a cell and the one above - for floors, flat roofs and landings; available from the start because a roof is what makes a shelter (building slice 2 un-gated it; the boss reward is the pitched roof wedge instead). Same thickness as a wall so a floor's rim and a wall's top meet cleanly.

Two half-height steps in one cell, rising toward the back; R turns them (an oriented block, one of two shapes that use the rotation key). A cube's cost for a cube's cell, so climbing your own building is never cheaper than building it.

A wall piece two cells tall (the player is 1.92 m) whose leaf swings open on E and closes again; while open its collision is gone and mobs may follow you through. Occupies the face it stands on and the one above, so nothing else can straddle the opening. R flips the hinge to the other side. Costs a cube: a door is the most valuable square metre of a shelter.

The visible reward for the first Forge Tyrant kill (trial.json completion_unlock): a 45-degree wedge filling a cell, low at the front and full height at the back, turned with R, so pitched roofs and ramps join the vocabulary. Flat roofs from slabs are always possible; the wedge is what makes a build look finished, which is the right kind of reward - it widens what can be built without gating shelter.

Fine mode's cube: one registry cell (half a build cell each way), the same rule at half the grid. Eight of them make a cube for four times the price - detail costs, bulk is cheap - so fine pieces are for trim, steps, sills and furniture, never for walls by the metre.
Fine mode's wall: a quarter of a panel on one registry face, for parapets, window sills, half-height partitions and patching the gap a full panel cannot fit.

Fine mode's post: half a cell tall on any registry edge, including the edges through the middle of a block's top face - the owner's 'a post on a block' at sub-block scale. Balusters, table legs, fence pickets.
Fine mode's beam: half a cell long on any horizontal registry edge, for rails, sills and the small lintel over a half-wall gap.
Fine mode's slab: a quarter of a floor on one registry face, for shelves, steps between half-cubes, and roof edges.

design_purpose: grid_size_metres balances Minecraft-like constraint against detail (final value is an open question in construction.md). placement_range_metres is measured from the third-person camera, which sits about 4.5 m behind the player, so it must cover that set-back plus reach; 6 m could not reach the floor in front of the player. removal_refund_fraction controls experimentation freedom versus commitment and deliberately mirrors salvage_return_fraction in crafting.json so building and crafting feel like one economy. element (block | wall | floor | post | beam) says which kind of lattice element a shape occupies: a block takes a whole cell, a wall a vertical face shared by two cells, a floor a horizontal face, a post a vertical edge shared by four cells, a beam a horizontal edge. Placement snaps to the nearest free element of that kind to the crosshair, and two pieces only conflict when they want the same element - which is what lets a cube sit against a wall, a post stand where two walls meet, and a slab rim carry a beam, with no slot bookkeeping and no rotation key for anything but oriented shapes. lattice_divisions is how much finer the occupancy registry is than the build grid (2 = half cells): full-size pieces occupy a footprint of registry elements, which is what lets half-scale pieces (fine mode) share the world with them through one set lookup. form (box | stairs | wedge | door, default box) picks the mesh and collision the engine builds; oriented (default false) says R turns the piece; cells_tall (default 1) stacks the footprint upward, for the two-cell door. fine (default false) marks a half-scale piece that occupies one registry element, and fine_of names the full-size shape it is the fine twin of: fine mode (G) swaps the selection for its twin and back, so the palette stays eight shapes with a scale toggle rather than thirteen.
